source.title: Encourage or Inhibit Monosemanticity? Revisit Monosemanticity from a Feature Decorrelation Perspective
source.authors: Hanqi Yan; Yanzheng Xiang; Guang-Yi Chen; Yifei Wang; Lin Gui; Yu-Lan He

record.tranche_reason: The study measures monosemanticity using activation-correlation proxies rather than interpreting individual neurons, and reports how the proxies change during preference optimization and regularization.
record.gate_note: The study reports monosemanticity-proxy results in Figures 3–5. Figure 6 measures activation sparsity, and Table 2 and Figure 7 report alignment and reward-margin outcomes; these do not directly measure polysemanticity or monosemanticity, so they are not rows. The paper also discusses superposition and cites prior neuron findings, but those are not new results from this study.
record.test_reason: The study never measures whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs, nor the share of such neurons. It tracks two proxies. One is Gurnee's weight-norm×bias product in GPT-2. The other is 'feature decorrelation': 1 − cosine similarity between activation vectors for different inputs in Llama-2-7b. The second measures representation diversity or token uniformity, not neuron polysemanticity. The work uses monosemanticity as motivation for its own regularizer (DecPO) and reports that method's alignment gains. This is a related but different construct, so no version is tested. The findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but incomplete. The authors conclude that DPO increases monosemanticity as measured by their proxies, and that there is no clear relation between monosemanticity and model size. They argue the inhibition conclusion of Wang et al. (2024) does not hold across models. They hold that monosemanticity should be encouraged, and propose a decorrelation regularizer (DecPO) that improves alignment and reward margin. They acknowledge the analysis is ad hoc and limited to Llama-family models up to 8B trained on limited data.
record.recipe_differences: Uses activation decorrelation and a weight-norm/bias proxy rather than interpreting individual neurons or applying the original neuron-level analysis. The regularizer is added to DPO.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported proxy varies by layer: DPO improves it in earlier GPT-2 layers but it declines in later layers. The Llama decorrelation curves also vary over training stage.

fits_no_version.finding: DPO raises the Gurnee weight-norm×bias superposition proxy in earlier layers of GPT-2 medium, large and xl (Fig. 3). The proxy declines in later layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preference optimization (DPO) changes layerwise superposition proxies in LMs, increasing proxy monosemanticity in early layers and decreasing it in late layers.

fits_no_version.finding: DPO, and more so the DecPO regularizer, increases 1 − cosine similarity between MLP activations of different inputs in Llama-2-7b. The rise comes early in training and is followed by a decline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preference optimization increases activation decorrelation (representation diversity) in LM MLPs; a decorrelation regularizer amplifies this and slows its later decline.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: Monosemanticity is inferred from proxies rather than neuron-level semantic interpretations. Several proxy outcomes are shown only in figures, without exact extracted values or uncertainty estimates. The authors also state that the analysis is ad hoc, uses limited data, and covers models from the same Llama family for their larger-model experiments.
record.rows_left_out: None of the direct proxy results in Figures 3–5 were left out. Figure 6's activation-variance/sparsity measure and Table 2/Figure 7 alignment and reward-margin results were omitted because they do not directly measure monosemanticity or polysemanticity.

untested.parts: No measure of how many LM MLP neurons respond to unrelated tokens or contexts.
Superposition is discussed theoretically only; capacity pressure is not tested.
Effects of training and regularization are tracked only via proxies. There is no neuron-level polysemanticity share. The ReLU swap collapsed the model and was not measured.
No inspection of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No comparison of activation ranges or explanation scoring.

missing.what: Cross-model layerwise weight-norm×bias proxy for GPT-2 medium/large/xl, GPT-neo-2.7B and GPT-J-6B. Authors find no consistent relation to model size.
missing.versions: none (proxy; would bear on a size/architecture claim only via proxy)

missing.what: Qualitative top-token mapping of predominant MLP dimensions by layer after DecPO. Deeper layers yield more concrete themes.
Replacing SiLU with ReLU caused model collapse. No polysemanticity measure is reported for it.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'supports V5' label rests entirely on proxies. The decorrelation proxy is a cross-input cosine measure that does not identify neurons responding to unrelated concepts. DecPO rows are the study's own method and directly optimize that proxy. The reader's limits_scope label miscasts the later-layer declines as 'partial' rather than as a reversal of the proxy.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifiers or vision neurons are studied.
The study does not measure whether language-model neurons respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, nor the share of such neurons.
The study discusses superposition and decorrelation, but does not test whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or whether models represent more sparse features than they have neurons.
The study does not test whether initialization, regularization, or training noise produces polysemantic neurons when capacity pressure is absent.

It tests DPO training and decorrelation regularization using activation-correlation proxies. It does not compare architectures or activation functions for their effect on neuron-level polysemanticity, test lowering polysemanticity, or establish that nearly all neurons retain coherent jobs without a performance cost.
The study does not inspect canonical polysemantic neurons or test whether their apparently mixed inputs share a feature.
It does not compare activation-range choices or explanation-scoring methods for deciding whether individual neurons count as polysemantic.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Earlier layers in the tested GPT-2 models, DPO on the three Llama-2-7b-hf datasets, and DPO or DecPO training on Toxicity
reader_labels.reason: The study reports increased monosemanticity proxies after DPO in earlier layers and increased feature decorrelation after DPO or DecPO; see r1, r3, r5, r7-r17.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Later layers in the tested GPT-2 models and across training stages
reader_labels.reason: The proxy declines in later GPT-2 layers, and the Llama training curves show a decrease after an early increase; see r2, r4, r6, r14-r17.
